images.caption: Figure 1:We proposeTCP4D, a unified model that tracks tool-center-point (TCP) poses and gripper states from RGB videos and generates task-conditioned future TCP trajectories and gripper states, enabling robot manipulation and cross-embodiment data augmentation.

Figure 2:Overview of TCP4D.\raisebox{0.2pt}{\scriptsize1}⃝
TCP4D Tracker takes a monocular video as input and constructs a 4D scene representation.
Given the TCP’s 2D location in the initial frame as a query, it decodes the scene geometry, the TCP’sSE⁡(3)\mathrm{SE}(3)motion, and the gripper state.
\raisebox{0.2pt}{\scriptsize2}⃝
TCP4D Generator extracts local features along the TCP tracks to form queries and incorporates the robot states.
Conditioned on the current 4D scene representation, the wrist RGB view, and language instruction, it predicts the TCP motion and gripper state over the nexthhsteps.

Figure 4:Qualitative comparison of TCP tracking.We compare TCP tracking by TCP4D against dense tracking baselines followed by post-processing.
The left side shows the input video.
The red point in the first frame marks the query used by TCP4D, while the green points indicate the rigid point group tracked by the baselines.
More visualizations are provided in Appx.D.8.

Figure 5:Example of our cross-embodiment augmented data.Given an RGB video, TCP4D reconstructs the TCP’s 3D trajectory and gripper state, enabling augmentation on any embodiment that satisfiesreachability.
More visualizations in Appx.B.

Figure 7:Real-world experiments setup and task rollouts.The right panel shows the rollout of tasks1) placing pensand2) stacking bowls, with the predicted TCP trajectory over the next 32 steps displayed in each inference window.
The color gradient from blue to orange indicates the temporal order of future actions.
Complete rollout visualizations are in Appx.F.2.

Figure 10:Sliding-window TCP tracking inference.TCP4D supports inference on sequences of varying lengths.
To track a long sequence, only the TCP’s 2D location in the first frame needs to be specified.
The predicted 3D TCP position,(x,y,z)(x,y,z), at the final frame can then be projected onto the camera plane and used as the new query for the next window.

Figure 11:Query points on DROID and Robolab for baseline evaluation.For baselines evaluated by rigid fitting of point tracks, we select 16 point groups on the gripper in the first frame of each window using ground-truth annotations, track them throughout the window, and fit the TCP pose from the tracked points.

Figure 12:Visualization of TCP4D for few-shot cross-embodiment adaptation.We fine-tune TCP4D using only three and ten randomly selected episodes for three-shot and ten-shot transfer, respectively.
The orange and green paths represent the predicted and ground-truth TCP trajectories, respectively.
Our method can be readily transferred to new environments and robot embodiments.
Figure 13:Qualitative results of TCP4D Tracker on real-world task.Methods such as 4RC and MOSE3 can experience tracking failures.
